Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones While Driving

Almost everyone carries a cell phone now, and most of us reach for it dozens of times a day without thinking. That habit is harmless on a couch or at a desk. Behind the wheel it is dangerous. Drivers should not be allowed to use handheld cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, and the law should treat the phone as the hazard that it is.

The central problem is attention. Driving looks automatic, but it demands constant judgment: watching the car ahead, checking mirrors, noticing a pedestrian at the curb, predicting what other drivers will do. A phone pulls on the same mental resources. Researchers usually describe three kinds of distraction: visual, when the eyes leave the road; manual, when the hands leave the wheel; and cognitive, when the mind leaves the task. Texting combines all three. A driver who glances at a message for five seconds while traveling at highway speed covers roughly the length of a football field without looking at the road. Nothing about a modern car makes up for that blindness.

The numbers back this up. Distracted driving kills thousands of people in the United States every year, and the true figure is probably higher than reported because drivers rarely admit to being on their phones after a crash. Many of the victims are not the distracted drivers at all. They are passengers, cyclists, children walking to school, and other motorists who did everything right. This is why the issue cannot be treated as a matter of personal freedom. A person who chooses to take a risk with his own life is one thing. A person who takes that risk with strangers' lives is another.

Some people argue that hands-free calling is safe enough, and that a ban should only cover texting. This sounds reasonable, but the evidence does not support it. Studies using driving simulators and real traffic data have found that the conversation itself is the distraction, not just the act of holding the phone. A driver deep in a phone call misses more traffic signals and reacts more slowly to sudden braking, even with both hands on the wheel and both eyes forward. The brain cannot fully give itself to a conversation and to the road at the same moment. It switches back and forth, and each switch costs time that a driver does not always have. Hands-free technology fixes the manual problem and leaves the cognitive one untouched.

Others say that drivers can already talk to passengers or change the radio, so phones are no different. But a passenger shares the road with the driver and tends to go quiet when traffic gets tense. A person on the other end of a phone line cannot see the intersection and keeps talking. A radio dial is also simple and brief, while a phone offers endless messages, notifications, and apps designed to hold attention. The phone is built to be hard to ignore, which is exactly the wrong quality for something inside a moving car.

Enforcement is a fair concern, since no law works if nobody follows it. Yet the history of seat belt laws and drunk driving laws shows that firm rules change behavior over time. When the penalties are real and the public understands the reason, what once seemed normal begins to feel irresponsible. A clear and complete rule is also easier to enforce than a patchwork of exceptions. If an officer sees a phone in a driver's hand, there is no need to guess whether the driver was dialing, reading, or doing something allowed.

There should be sensible exceptions. A driver facing a real emergency, such as reporting a crash or calling for help, should be able to do so, and a navigation screen set up before the trip begins is reasonable. Parking the car and then using the phone is always an option. These exceptions are narrow, and they do not weaken the main point: a trip in a car is not the time for calls, texts, or scrolling.

Nobody needs to be reachable every minute of the day. Arriving a little later, or letting a message wait, costs almost nothing. The alternative can cost a life. Drivers should put the phone away until the car is parked, and the law should require it.
